figures.caption: Fig. 1. (a) Schematic of the DEM microstructure generation process, from initial random packing to final compacted electrode structure, demonstrating the CAM particles (black) and SE particles (yellow). After reaching the prescribed pressure, the achieved microstructural data is used for our evaluations, considering the target SE particles (red) which are contact with the SE separator layer (yellow sheet). (b) Workflow comparison between the FEM and RNM modeling approaches. The FEM pipeline (top) involves SE phase extraction, meshing, and electrostatic simulation to compute the potential field and effective ionic conductivity. In contrast, the RNM pipeline (bottom) bypasses geometric meshing and directly solves the resistor network formed by SE particle contacts. figures.caption: Fig. 4. Electrochemical impedance spectra (hollow dots) and corresponding transmission line model (TLM) fits (dashed lines) for full-blocking cells assem- bled with composite cathodes containing 𝑓CAM = 70, 75, and 80 wt.%. The spectra reflect the ionic transport behavior through the SE network within the cathode microstructure. An equivalent TLM circuit was used to extract the effective ionic conductivity 𝜎eff,ion for each composition.

figures.caption: Fig. 5. Convergence behavior of 𝜎eff,ion as a function of box factor for (a–c) Finite Element Modeling and (d–f) Resistor Network Modeling at 70, 75, and 80 wt.% 𝑓CAM, respectively. Each distribution represents 10 independently extracted RVEs. Beyond raw simulation time, RNM holds additional computational advantages. Unlike FEM, which requires preprocessing steps such as SE phase preparation and mesh generation (not included in the timing analysis), RNM operates directly on particle-level data. This distinc- tion is also illustrated in the workflow schematic (Fig. 1) (b), where the more streamlined RNM path bypasses time-intensive volumetric meshing steps required for FEM. This drastically reduces total work- flow time and simplifies automation for high-throughput simulations. figures.caption: Fig. 6. (a) Average number of SE particles within the RVE as a function of box factor, showing a monotonic increase due to volumetric scaling. (b) Average simulation time required for FEM and RNM solvers as a function of box factor for different CAM contents. RNM exhibits significantly shorter simulation times than FEM across all cases. (c) Comparison of effective ionic conductivity 𝜎eff,ion extracted from experimental full-blocking EIS measurements, Finite Element Modeling (FEM), and Resistor Network Modeling (RNM) for composite cath- odes with 𝑓CAM = 70, 75, and 80 wt.%.

figures.caption: Fig. 7. Effective ionic conductivity 𝜎eff,ion as a function of mean SE particle size 𝐷SE and 𝑓CAM computed using (a) FEM and (b) RNM. SE network descriptors as a function of 𝐷SE and 𝑓CAM: (c) SE utilization 𝜃SE, (d) SE–SE coordination number 𝑍SE−SE, and (e) average SE–SE contact resistance ̄𝑅SE−SE. Fig. 8 summarizes the results from the RNM calculations. As shown in Fig. 8(a), 𝜎eff,ion increases monotonically with pressure across all compositions. This trend is attributed to enhanced particle packing and improved SE–SE contact formation, leading to more effective percola- tion. From 100 to 400 MPa, the absolute and relative improvements are +0.067 mS/cm (98%) for 70 wt.%, +0.044 mS/cm (126%) for 75 wt.%, and +0.023 mS/cm (291%) for 80 wt.%. Although the relative gain is largest at 80 wt.% due to a poorly connected initial network, the highest absolute values are still reached at 70 wt.%,

figures.caption: Fig. 8. Pressure-dependent properties of the SE phase evaluated using resistor network modeling (RNM): (a) effective ionic conductivity 𝜎eff,ion, (b) SE-utilization 𝜃SE, (c) average SE–SE contact resistance ̄𝑅SE−SE, and (d) SE–SE coordination number 𝑍SE−SE as a function of compaction pressure for cathodes with 𝑓CAM = 70, 75, and 80 wt.%. While FEM offers high-fidelity spatial resolution, RNM provided similar accuracy at drastically reduced computational cost — up to two orders of magnitude faster — without requiring mesh generation or SE phase preparation. This makes RNM especially suitable for large-scale parametric studies and high-throughput screening. pathways alongside ionic conduction for a more comprehensive rep- resentation of the composite cathode.
